title: Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards
backgroundAndFacts:
The H-2A visa program allows American agricultural employers to hire temporary foreign workers when there are not enough domestic workers available. In exchange for this privilege, employers must follow strict rules protecting both the foreign guest workers and any American workers doing similar jobs — covering wages, housing, transportation, and working conditions. The Department of Labor (DOL) is responsible for enforcing these rules and, when employers violate them, can seek to recover back wages and other monetary penalties on behalf of affected workers.

Sun Valley Orchards is a New Jersey farm that the Department of Labor accused of violating H-2A program requirements. Rather than filing a lawsuit in federal court, the DOL initiated an administrative enforcement proceeding — meaning the case was heard by an administrative law judge employed by the agency itself, not an independent Article III federal judge. Sun Valley challenged this process, arguing that the Constitution requires monetary claims like these to be decided by a real federal court with an independent judge, not by an in-house government tribunal.

The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit sided with Sun Valley, ruling that the Department of Labor's in-house adjudication of monetary remedies against employers violated Article III of the Constitution, which vests the judicial power of the United States exclusively in federal courts whose judges enjoy life tenure and salary protections. The Supreme Court then agreed to hear the government's appeal, also taking up the separate question of whether the immigration statute that created the H-2A program actually gives the DOL the legal authority to conduct such proceedings in the first place.
legalQuestion: Whether the Constitution's Article III and federal immigration law permit the Department of Labor to conduct its own internal hearings to order employers to pay money damages for violations of H-2A agricultural guest worker program requirements, rather than requiring those cases to go before a federal court.
significance:
This case sits at the intersection of administrative law, constitutional separation of powers, and immigration enforcement, making it one of the most consequential regulatory cases in years. At stake is whether federal executive agencies can act as judge and jury when seeking to extract money from private parties — a practice that is widespread across the federal government, used not just by the DOL but by dozens of agencies including the SEC, FTC, NLRB, and EPA. A ruling against the government could force a massive restructuring of how federal agencies enforce the law, requiring them to bring monetary claims in Article III courts rather than in their own tribunals.

The case also has direct practical implications for the H-2A agricultural guest worker program, which has grown dramatically in recent years and is relied upon by farms across the country. If the DOL loses its adjudicative authority, enforcement of worker protections for hundreds of thousands of seasonal agricultural workers could be significantly weakened or delayed. Conversely, a ruling for the government could be seen as endorsing broad executive agency power at a time when courts are already reconsidering the scope of the administrative state.

parties.party: Department of Labor and Lori Chavez-DeRemer, Secretary of Labor
parties.coreArgument: Congress expressly authorized the DOL to adjudicate H-2A enforcement proceedings through the immigration statute, and such adjudication does not violate Article III because it falls within well-recognized exceptions that allow Congress to assign certain public rights disputes to administrative agencies rather than Article III courts.
supportingPoints: The H-2A program created a government-benefit scheme with conditions, and enforcement of those conditions involves 'public rights' that Congress may assign to administrative adjudication without violating Article III.
The statute at 8 U.S.C. §1188(g)(2) grants the DOL broad authority to 'take such other administrative action' as necessary to enforce employer obligations, which fairly encompasses monetary remedies.

Decades of settled practice have permitted federal agencies to adjudicate monetary claims in enforcement of regulatory programs, and disrupting this would cause enormous disruption to federal enforcement across many agencies.

The Third Circuit's ruling is inconsistent with Supreme Court precedents recognizing the government's authority to use administrative tribunals for enforcement of conditions attached to participation in federal regulatory programs.

parties.coreArgument: The Constitution's Article III requires that private parties facing government demands for money judgments have their cases heard before an independent federal judge, not an executive-branch employee, and the H-2A statute does not clearly grant the DOL authority to adjudicate such monetary claims in the first place.
supportingPoints: When the government seeks to take money from a private employer as a legal remedy, that is a classic exercise of judicial power that must be performed by an Article III court with an independent, tenured judge — not an agency employee.

The 'public rights' exception to Article III is narrow and does not apply here because Sun Valley's liability sounds in private common-law obligations, not the administration of a government-benefit scheme.

The statutory text of 8 U.S.C. §1188(g)(2) does not clearly authorize monetary adjudication by the agency, and courts should not read ambiguous statutes to grant agencies such constitutionally significant power.

Allowing agencies to serve as both prosecutor and judge in monetary enforcement actions creates an intolerable conflict of interest and denies employers the neutral adjudicator guaranteed by due process and Article III.

citedPrecedents.reasonCited: This recent ruling that the SEC could not use in-house tribunals to adjudicate certain fraud penalties is the most directly on-point precedent and provides the analytical framework the Court will likely apply to the H-2A enforcement context.

Establishes that Article III limits Congress's ability to strip federal courts of jurisdiction over claims that are traditionally resolved in courts of law, relevant to whether monetary H-2A enforcement claims belong in agency or Article III proceedings.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Atlas Roofing Co. v. Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: Held that Congress may assign adjudication of certain statutory penalties to administrative agencies without a jury trial, which the government argues supports its authority to adjudicate H-2A monetary remedies in-house.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Murray's Lessee v. Hoboken Land & Improvement Co.
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: One of the foundational cases defining the scope of 'public rights' that Congress may assign to non-Article III adjudication, relevant to determining whether H-2A enforcement falls within that category.

A landmark case on the limits of congressional power to assign adjudication to administrative agencies, establishing that certain 'private rights' require Article III adjudication — a distinction central to the dispute over H-2A enforcement.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Oil States Energy Services v. Greene's Energy Group
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: Clarified the public rights doctrine by holding that patent validity — a matter arising from a federal regulatory scheme — could be adjudicated by an executive agency, offering the government a template for arguing H-2A enforcement is similarly a public right.
